case_study_insert.main_stem: Wessex Steam Railway (WSR) is a cooperative in the tourism and heritage sector in Somerset, employing a workforce of 28 paid staff plus volunteers. Founded in 1969 by Gerald Penfold, it uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and elected trustees. WSR plans to invest $560,000 in a new locomotive shed and visitor centre, financed by a $360,000 bank loan and $200,000 of retained surplus built up over many years. It has fixed costs of $170,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $52, and produces 11,000 units a year in passenger journeys. WSR faces falling volunteer numbers and complaints about cancelled services during the summer season.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — 2025 Season: WSR carried 2,750 passengers on 120 operating days, with 9 services cancelled because of locomotive faults, up from 3 last year. Complaints rose from 8 to 22 per month; 51% of a 200-visitor survey wanted more frequent trains. Average journey length was 38 minutes. Ten of 28 paid staff and volunteers left; a signalling course costs $640 per person while on-the-job training with senior drivers is free. A $2 ticket-price rise was trialled.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Wessex Steam Railway as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Heritage Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.0% to 4.75%, raising loan interest. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.4% from $12.80 to $13.62 per hour from April 2026. (3) Coal, fuel and maintenance input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while consumer spending on heritage tourism grew 5.2%.

questions.question_text: WSR plans to fund part of its $560,000 locomotive shed and visitor centre with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for WSR of using the $200,000 retained surplus instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Spending the $200,000 retained surplus avoids interest charges and capital repayments, so WSR's cash flow is protected while it already meets fixed costs of $170,000 a year. Money not paid to a lender can be used to reduce the 9 cancelled services and the 22 monthly complaints, protecting the $52 ticket price and the 11,000 passenger journeys sold.

Point 2: Using its own surplus keeps the new locomotive shed and visitor centre owned by the cooperative and its elected trustees, with no need to pledge assets as collateral and no risk of repossession if passenger numbers fall short. This suits a flat structure with democratic leadership, where members decide how the $560,000 investment is used without lender conditions. The smaller $360,000 loan that remains is easier to service from the $34 contribution on each journey.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained surplus over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to WSR's $200,000 retained surplus, $560,000 investment and cash flow.

questions.question_text: WSR wants to raise passenger numbers at the new visitor centre. Consider partnerships with local museums and printed leaflets, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should WSR choose to promote the visitor centre? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Museum partnerships and printed leaflets: Linking with Somerset museums and leaving leaflets at heritage sites can reach tourists already interested in steam and history, at low cost, and fits WSR's cooperative roots. It suits the 51% of 200 surveyed visitors who wanted more frequent trains by promoting a fuller timetable. The approach is slow, however, and leaflet distribution is hard to measure, so it may not fill the new centre quickly enough to justify $560,000.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio around Somerset is affordable and reaches the local catchment that supplies much of the 2,750 passenger trade, and it works for short-notice messages about special steam events. Its reach is narrow, however, and cannot tap the 5.2% growth in heritage tourism spending from visitors travelling further afield, so it is best used as support.

Social media influencer marketing: Heritage and family-travel influencers can show the new shed and centre to exactly the tourism audience that is growing, at low cost per booking and with measurable engagement. Content can highlight the 38-minute journeys and address the 22 monthly complaints about cancellations by showing reliability improvements. Results build gradually and depend on authentic storytellers.

Recommendation: WSR should choose social media influencer marketing, backed by museum leaflets. Social media reaches the growing heritage market cost-effectively; radio is rejected as too narrow for a $560,000 visitor centre, and leaflets alone are rejected as slow and hard to measure, so they are used only as a local supplement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States simple promotional ideas with little reference to WSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WSR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of WSR's visitors, complaints and investment with a justified recommendation that rejects the alternatives.

questions.question_text: WSR faces falling volunteer numbers and complaints about cancelled services. Explain two benefits for WSR of its democratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 28 paid staff, volunteers and elected trustees a say in rostering and locomotive maintenance, which raises commitment and helps reverse the ten departures and falling volunteer numbers. Involved volunteers are more likely to turn up reliably, reducing the 9 cancelled services and the 22 monthly complaints, protecting the 2,750 passengers carried.

Point 2: Because WSR has a flat structure, ideas from drivers and volunteers reach decisions quickly, so the fault causing cancellations can be fixed without layers of approval. This protects the 38-minute journey experience and the 51% of surveyed visitors who want more frequent trains, supporting the $52 fare and the $34 contribution per journey while the $560,000 visitor centre is developed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WSR's volunteers, cancellations, complaints and fares.

questions.question_text: WSR must improve reliability and skills among its drivers. Consider a signalling course at $640 per person or free on-the-job training with senior drivers. Which should WSR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Signalling course: A $640 course gives formal signalling knowledge and a recognised qualification for the ten people who left or need upgrading, helping prevent the 9 cancelled services and the 22 monthly complaints. The total for ten is $6,400, small beside a $560,000 investment. The drawback is that trainees are away from the railway, reducing capacity during the 120 operating days, and generic content may not cover WSR's exact steam procedures.

On-the-job training: Senior drivers can teach signalling on WSR's own locomotives at no cash cost, keeping trains running and passing on heritage-specific knowledge, which suits a cooperative with a flat structure and elected trustees. It avoids the $6,400 spend and suits volunteers who leave quickly. However, it uses senior drivers' time, can spread bad habits, and gives no certificate, a risk when 51% of visitors want more reliable, frequent trains.

Decision: WSR should choose on-the-job training for routine instruction, with $640 signalling courses for those taking responsibility for trains. Coaching is free, locomotive-specific and avoids removing staff from the 120-day season. Full external training is rejected because $6,400 and lost operating days would cut the 2,750 passengers, while coaching alone is rejected because it lacks formal certification for safety-critical signalling.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little reference to WSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of WSR's costs and reliability.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in the context of WSR with a justified decision covering certification, cost and operating days.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WSR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $170,000 ÷ ($52 − $18) = $170,000 ÷ $34 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 passenger journeys a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $52 − $18 = $34. Answer: contribution per unit is $34.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WSR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with 11,000 journeys sold to confirm the railway is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 6,000 journeys, which supports the $560,000 visitor centre.
2. Use the $34 contribution to model the $2 price rise trialled: at $54, contribution becomes $36 and break-even falls to $170,000 ÷ $36 = 4,722 journeys, showing the benefit of a small fare increase.
3. Use fixed costs of $170,000 and $34 contribution to set the passenger target needed to service the $360,000 loan on the new shed.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($170,000 ÷ 11,000 + $18 = $33.45 a journey) to detect waste behind the 9 cancelled services and judge whether the $18 variable cost is rising with 8.7% coal, fuel and maintenance inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $34 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 6,000 against 11,000 journeys; modelling the $2 fare rise; loan-service target for the $360,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $33.45 to monitor cancellations and fuel costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WSR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WSR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.79 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $15,000 inventories + $30,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $90,000; 2025 current assets = $20,000 + $45,000 + $60,000 = $125,000. 2024 short-term cover = $90,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $125,000 ÷ $70,000 = 1.79. The inventory-excluding measure for 2024 = ($90,000 − $15,000) ÷ $60,000 = $75,000 ÷ $60,000 = 1.25; for 2025 = ($125,000 − $20,000) ÷ $70,000 = $105,000 ÷ $70,000 = 1.50.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved strongly. Cover of short-term obligations rose from 1.50 to 1.79 because current assets grew from $90,000 to $125,000 while current liabilities rose only from $60,000 to $70,000. Cash increased from $45,000 to $60,000, giving WSR real funds to handle the 9 cancelled services and fund repairs, and the inventory-excluding measure rose from 1.25 to 1.50, so the improvement does not depend on selling stock. This is valuable while the cooperative plans a $560,000 shed and visitor centre and has a $360,000 loan.

Conclusion: WSR's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.50 to 1.79) and the acid test ratio (1.25 to 1.50) show stronger short-term solvency, backed by higher cash. The main caution is that trade receivables rose from $30,000 to $45,000, so credit control should still be watched, but overall the cooperative is better placed to invest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WSR of raising the $52 ticket price by $2 to fund locomotive maintenance.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The $2 rise from $52 to $54 increases contribution per journey from $34 to $36, giving extra funds for the maintenance behind 9 cancelled services and the 22 monthly complaints. With fixed costs of $170,000 and 11,000 journeys, the additional contribution helps service the $360,000 loan and supports the $560,000 shed without more borrowing.

Disadvantage: The 200-visitor survey showed 51% wanted more frequent trains rather than higher prices, so a fare rise could deter families and reduce the 2,750 passengers carried. As a cooperative relying on volunteers and a workforce of 28, WSR may also face resentment if visitors feel a heritage service is becoming too commercial, and the $640 training needs would still have to be funded.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WSR's fare, cancellations, survey and loans.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in input costs will affect WSR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If WSR's $360,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $360,000 = $2,700 a year (0.0075 × $360,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $170,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no extra cost. Higher rates may also trim heritage-tourism spending, but WSR can largely remove the financing risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.62 per hour): With a workforce of 28 paid staff, some roles are hourly paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented. The honest test is given productivity: 11,000 journeys ÷ 28 staff = about 393 journeys per worker, so the rise is manageable only if productivity holds or passenger numbers grow; otherwise the $34 contribution per journey shrinks.

Input cost inflation (8.7% in coal, fuel and maintenance): The $18 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7%, that adds 8.7% × $18 = $1.57 a journey, or about $17,270 a year at 11,000 journeys (11,000 × $1.57). Even a smaller rise would reduce the $34 contribution, and it hits every journey at a time when 9 services were cancelled for locomotive faults.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 11,000 journeys and directly erodes the $34 contribution needed for the $560,000 visitor centre. The interest rise is only about $2,700 and can be fixed, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity of about 393 journeys per worker, whereas fuel and maintenance inflation has no immediate offset.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies external changes with limited application to WSR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on WSR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of WSR with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
